extracted.intended_audience: first-year Cambridge mathematicians (and similar undergraduate math students)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for first-year Cambridge undergraduates on how to study mathematics effectively: preparing for supervisions, reading lecture notes, learning to prove results, time management, and use of online resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give clear motivation for topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a clear idea why you are making the effort to learn a topic (not merely ‘to do well in exams’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecturers and textbooks often assume a topic is interesting/important; learners should actively ask "why does this matter?" to motivate study and understand context. This aids engagement and deeper understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn to come up with proofs yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop the ability to work out proofs (possibly with small hints) rather than merely memorizing them from lectures/notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being able to reconstruct proofs reduces the burden on memory and helps with example sheets; the blog's main theme is to teach methods for discovering routine proofs. Practice attempting proofs before reading provided solutions; use hints sparingly so you retain only the hint rather than the whole proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for supervisions (don’t leave sheets until the last minute)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do serious, advance preparation for supervisions rather than leaving example sheets to the day or evening before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have seriously thought about a question, a supervisor’s explanation can create an AHA! moment. Last-minute preparation leads to skipping hard questions and missing the learning opportunity. Specific suggestions: (i) don't leave sheets to the deadline; (ii) if you're not on top of the relevant course section, read and understand notes before attempting the sheet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fake difficulties — check definitions and background first
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish genuine mathematical difficulty from 'fake difficulty' caused by not knowing or checking definitions/results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fake difficulty example: saying 'I didn't know where to start' when you hadn't looked up a definition. If you don’t know a definition, look it up (notes, Wikipedia). Fake difficulties waste supervision time and prevent you engaging with real problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be active in supervisions — seek methods not just answers
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't be satisfied with being shown answers; aim to learn general methods that you can reuse in future situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a supervisor shows a trick or a step, ask how they thought of it or why that method is natural. If a supervisor suggests proving a lemma first, ask for the general message: 'In this kind of situation, the following method often works.' This helps convert a single example into a transferable technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t be passive when reading lecture notes — try to predict and prove
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage actively with notes: try to guess what's coming next and attempt proofs yourself before reading them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat note-reading like a conversation: anticipate statements, guess the role of lemmas, and attempt proofs until genuinely stuck. When stuck, put in enough effort to determine the genuine difficulty, then peek for a hint. Remembering a small hint is easier than memorizing a whole proof (analogy: substitute 'mouse' for 'mat').

rubrics_metrics.name: Read and digest lecture notes between lectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Read your notes soon after lectures and make sure you understand them rather than just copying them down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding notes between lectures makes subsequent lectures easier to follow, reduces time needed to digest future lectures, simplifies example sheets, and saves time overall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be organized with your time
rubrics_metrics.description: Good organization and time management save time in the long run; avoid leaving things to the last minute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although hard, organization means the time spent preparing yields greater future returns (more work before supervision saves more time later). Procrastination forces more total work to reach the same standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that mathematics gets hard and respond by working
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that encountering hard material is normal and not a personal failing; respond by developing effective study habits and putting in work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some students find courses hard earlier than others; the right response is disciplined work and habit formation. The post emphasizes that mathematical ability is largely acquired through sustained effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use online resources intelligently (Wikipedia, Math.StackExchange, quizzes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the internet to look up definitions, ask precise questions on Math.StackExchange, and practise basics with quizzes like Terence Tao’s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you don't understand part of a course, formulate a precise question before posting; good questions are likely answered quickly. Be cautious of over-relying on copying solutions from ProofWiki/online sources — use them to understand context and deployment of ideas, not to shortcut learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: When short on time, reverse-engineer proofs efficiently
rubrics_metrics.description: If you lack time to rederive everything, read proofs, extract key novel steps, and reverse-engineer the argument to reconstitute it later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical strategy (from comments): read the whole proof, separate novel ideas from routine steps, record the key ideas, then attempt to reconstruct the proof using those ideas. This is a time-efficient way to gain understanding and creates effective revision notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be honest and explicit about gaps in solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate which parts of your solutions you think are suspect or incomplete when handing them in for supervision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than obfuscate gaps or feign understanding, flag potentially weak solutions so supervisors know where to focus. It's counterproductive to pretend deep thought when you don’t understand; supervisors can help best when you’re candid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t perform for appearance — focus on genuine learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid attempts to give the impression of deep thought or competence when you lack understanding; such behaviour wastes everyone's time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supervisors easily detect faked deliberation. Better to be straightforward about where you’re stuck and to ask clear questions that target your genuine difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use peers and cross-college resources (networking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make friends with students in other colleges/years to learn about useful books, notes, and supervisory practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer networks can point you to excellent notes or alternative explanations and provide emotional support. The comment thread emphasizes the value of informal sharing of resources.
